strengths: Addresses a practical problem of LoRA transferability across model variants with growing LLM ecosystem
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (BBH, MMLU, LaMP) and transfer settings (same model, cross-family, different sizes, different versions)
Practical contribution: avoids training an additional discriminator model, reducing computational overhead compared to TransLoRA
Thoughtful solution for tokenizer mismatches between source and target models with dual-pointer alignment algorithm
Strong experimental hygiene with thorough ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Consistent improvements across diverse scenarios (+4-8% average gains)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and commitment to release code
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is replacing a learned discriminator with a hand-crafted metric (loss difference). The term 'contrastive excess' is poorly motivated and has weak connection to actual contrastive learning.
Modest empirical improvements over TransLoRA (often 1-2%), with some results comparable to or worse than baselines (e.g., Llama3 3B→8B on MMLU)

Requires task-specific hyperparameter tuning: token selection ratio k% varies significantly (70% for most tasks, 30% for others), contradicting claims of simplicity; no principled guidance provided for new tasks

Weak theoretical justification: why should loss difference between models with/without LoRA identify task-relevant tokens? The provided intuition is informal and doesn't address counterexamples where confident backbone tokens could receive high scores

Incomplete experimental analysis: (1) LaMP limited to 2/7 tasks; (2) tokenizer alignment mechanism presented but not rigorously evaluated; (3) computational cost vs TransLoRA not compared; (4) missing comparisons with adapter merging baselines
Synthetic data still depends on 5 seed prompts; no sensitivity analysis to number/quality of seed prompts or performance when source model is weaker than target
Weak-to-strong transfer results suggest limited generalization: different k% needed for reasoning vs personalization tasks, and improvements smaller than within-model transfer
Presentation issues: Figure 1 cluttered; terminology choices ('contrastive excess') poorly motivated; unclear guidance on hyperparameter selection for new problems

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem of transferring LoRA adapters across models without original training data
Elegant and intuitive contrastive excess mechanism that eliminates need for discriminator model, simplifying over TransLoRA
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks and four diverse transfer scenarios with thorough ablations
Consistent improvements across all settings (+7.96% vs vanilla, +6.0% vs KD, +4.4% vs TransLoRA), with particularly strong gains on personalization tasks (+8.9-16.6%)
Clear presentation with detailed implementation details and thoughtful design choices (e.g., using source model for query generation)
Practical robustness demonstrated through tokenizer alignment algorithm, transfer with external data, and varied model families/sizes
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty - primarily combines existing ideas (synthetic data from TransLoRA, token selection from prior work) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Weak theoretical justification - no rigorous explanation for why loss difference correlates with task-relevant knowledge importance; connection between 'excess' and 'informativeness' is assumed rather than proven
Contradicts data-independence claim by requiring 5 seed prompts; comparison with KD(5-shot) in Table 6 is not entirely fair as TITOK benefits from synthetic expansion

Task-dependent hyperparameter tuning required - optimal k% varies by setting (70% vs 30%), suggesting method sensitivity and undermining 'lightweight' claim; no principled approach provided for k% selection
Limited architectural and scale diversity - all experiments on Mistral/Llama 3B-8B range; no evaluation on other architectures (GPT, Qwen) or larger models (13B+, 70B)

Missing statistical rigor - no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; some improvements are modest and potentially within noise levels (e.g., Table 1: Llama3 3B→8B on MMLU shows identical 0.475 for both methods)
Tokenizer alignment algorithm lacks principled justification - four rules appear ad-hoc with no comparison to alternatives or ablation study of alignment component
Incomplete analysis - no investigation of failure modes, insufficient analysis of what excess scores actually capture, limited exploration of weak-to-strong transfer behavior

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: LoRA adapter transfer across models is a genuine limitation with increasing importance
Clean, intuitive core idea: token-wise contrastive excess scores provide reasonable signal for identifying task-relevant tokens, with theoretical grounding in LLR and Neyman-Pearson lemma
Practical advantage over TransLoRA: eliminates separate discriminator model, achieving 1.5-2.5× speedup with comparable/better performance

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple transfer scenarios (same-family, cross-family, different sizes/versions), three diverse benchmarks, extensive ablations (Table 2), sensitivity analyses (Table 12), and robustness checks (external data, synthetic data quality, weak source models)
Strong robustness demonstrations: works with external data, low-quality synthetic data, different tokenizers, and weaker source models than target baseline
Excellent reproducibility support: detailed implementation, hyperparameters, code availability, extensive appendices
Consistent improvements across settings: 4-10% average gains over baselines in most scenarios
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: comparing expert vs. base model predictions is relatively straightforward; applying it to token selection is incremental extension of existing selective training work

Modest improvements in key scenarios: +4.75% over TransLoRA for same-family, 2-3% for weak-to-strong transfers, sometimes within standard deviation ranges (Table 11), insufficient to strongly justify added complexity

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: k% requires per-setting tuning (30% for Llama3 3B→8B vs. 70% default); Table 12 shows large performance variance (0.401-0.445 on BBH Mistral→Mistral across k%), contradicting 'not overly sensitive' claim

Continued dependence on synthetic data quality: despite 'data-free' framing, method requires source model synthetic generation; Table 17 shows quality varies (2.01-2.40/5.0) but sensitivity insufficiently analyzed; only one ablation (Table 14) on low-quality data

Unfair experimental comparisons: TransLoRA baseline modified to use source-generated queries (vs. original target-generated), conflating contributions; artificial 90/10 splits on test-only benchmarks reduce generalization claims
Limited architectural scope: evaluation only on Mistral/Llama families; no evaluation on other LLM architectures, reducing claims of generality

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: qualitative examples (Figure 5) superficial; no analysis of whether selected tokens capture semantic vs. syntactic information or what LoRA knowledge actually transfers; 'task-relevant' claims lack supporting evidence
Theoretical gaps: LLR connection not formally proven for transfer optimization; claims about 'maximal teacher-student divergence and larger gradients' need careful justification

Tokenizer alignment ad-hoc: averaging fractional scores in one-to-many/many-to-one cases could lose information; limited analysis of why averaging works; Table 7 shows degradation but insufficient explanation
Missing critical ablations: no comparison to naive baseline (synthetic data without filtering); seed prompt sensitivity (fixed at 5) not explored; 2× synthetic pool multiplier not justified
Limited scope: LaMP uses only 2/7 tasks; specific to LoRA, unclear applicability to other PEFT methods (prefix tuning, adapters)

Presentation issues: 30-page paper with extensive appendices is lengthy; some marketing language ('simple yet powerful'); distinction from prior selective training work could be sharper in introduction
